items.q: A 32-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation presents with sudden onset of bright red, painless vaginal bleeding while resting. Her abdomen is soft, non-tender, and the uterus is completely relaxed. Fetal heart rate is 142 bpm. What physical examination maneuver is strictly contraindicated at this stage?
items.exp: In any patient presenting with antepartum haemorrhage, a digital vaginal examination (per vaginum exam) is strictly contraindicated until placenta previa has been definitively excluded by ultrasound. Inserting a finger into the cervix can dislodge the placenta and precipitate catastrophic, life-threatening maternal hemorrhage.
r: Correct. Digital vaginal examination is strictly contraindicated prior to excluding placenta previa.
Incorrect. Speculum examination can be performed carefully after placenta previa is localized or ruled out.
Incorrect. Abdominal palpation is safe and confirms a soft non-tender uterus.
Incorrect. Transabdominal/transvaginal ultrasound is the primary diagnostic investigation.
items.kp: Digital vaginal examination is strictly contraindicated in antepartum haemorrhage until placenta previa is ruled out by ultrasound.

items.q: What is the single greatest risk factor for the development of placenta accreta spectrum (placenta accreta, increta, or percreta)?
o: Prior cesarean delivery in the presence of an overlying anterior placenta previa
Maternal grand multiparity without prior surgery
Advanced maternal age over 40 years alone
items.exp: The strongest risk factor for placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) is a history of prior cesarean delivery combined with an anterior placenta previa overlying the uterine scar. The risk rises progressively from ~3% with one prior cesarean, to 11% with two, 40% with three, and exceeds 60% with four or more prior cesarean deliveries.
r: Correct. A prior cesarean scar beneath an anterior placenta previa carries the highest risk of placenta accreta spectrum.
Incorrect. Grand multiparity is a minor risk factor compared to prior hysterotomy scars.
Incorrect. Advanced maternal age is a minor risk factor.
Incorrect. Gestational diabetes is unrelated to defective decidualization.
items.kp: Prior cesarean delivery with an overlying placenta previa is the single strongest risk factor for placenta accreta spectrum.

items.q: A 28-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks gestation with chronic hypertension presents with sudden, severe continuous lower abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding. On examination, the uterus is tense, rigid ('woody'), and exquisitely tender to palpation. Fetal heart sounds are absent. Coagulation profile shows fibrinogen of 90 mg/dL (normal > 200). What is the diagnosis?
o: Severe abruptio placentae with disseminated intravascular coagulation
items.exp: Severe abruptio placentae is characterized by painful dark bleeding, a hypertonic 'woody' tender uterus, fetal demise, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (hypofibrinogenemia < 100 mg/dL, elevated D-dimer). Retroplacental hematoma releases tissue factor/thromboplastin into maternal circulation, consuming clotting factors.
r: Correct. Severe pain, hypertonic woody uterus, fetal demise, and low fibrinogen define severe abruptio placentae with DIC.
Incorrect. Placenta previa features painless bleeding and a soft non-tender uterus.
Incorrect. Uterine rupture presents with loss of uterine contour and recession of presenting part in scarred uterus.
Incorrect. Appendicitis does not produce dark vaginal bleeding, uterine rigidity, or severe DIC.
items.kp: Abruptio placentae presents with painful bleeding, woody uterine rigidity, and thromboplastin-mediated DIC.

items.q: During emergency cesarean delivery for severe abruptio placentae, the obstetrician observes widespread purplish-blue, bruised discoloration across the myometrium and beneath the uterine serosa caused by extravasation of blood into the myometrial bundles. What is this clinical finding?
items.exp: Couvelaire uterus (uteroplacental apoplexy) is a complication of severe concealed abruptio placentae in which retroplacental hemorrhage dissects through the myometrium beneath the uterine serosa and into the broad ligaments, imparting a mottled, purplish, ecchymotic appearance. It is managed conservatively with uterotonics; hysterectomy is required only if intractable uterine atony persists.
r: Correct. Couvelaire uterus is widespread myometrial hematoma extravasation following severe abruption.
Incorrect. Bandl ring is a pathological retraction ring in obstructed labor.
Incorrect. Placenta percreta is invasion of chorionic villi through the uterine serosa.
Incorrect. Asherman syndrome is intrauterine adhesions.
items.kp: Couvelaire uterus is myometrial extravasation of blood causing purplish discoloration in severe abruptio placentae.

items.q: A woman in active labor at 39 weeks undergoes artificial rupture of membranes. Immediately following amniotomy, there is a gush of blood-stained amniotic fluid accompanied by acute fetal bradycardia dropping to 70 bpm with a sinusoidal pattern on CTG. The mother remains hemodynamically stable. What is the suspected diagnosis?
o: Vasa previa with ruptured fetal vessel
items.exp: Vasa previa occurs when fetal vessels unsupported by Wharton jelly course through the membranes across the internal cervical os (associated with velamentous cord insertion or succenturiate placental lobes). Membrane rupture lacerates these fetal vessels, causing rapid fetal exsanguination presenting as acute fetal bradycardia or sinusoidal FHR pattern. Immediate emergency cesarean section is lifesaving.
r: Correct. Gush of blood with immediate fetal bradycardia upon membrane rupture indicates ruptured vasa previa.
Incorrect. Abruption causes maternal pain, uterine rigidity, and maternal hemodynamic instability.
Incorrect. Uterine inversion occurs in the third stage of labor, causing neurogenic shock.
Incorrect. Amniotic fluid embolism causes sudden maternal cardiovascular collapse, hypoxia, and arrest.
items.kp: Vasa previa presents with acute fetal bleeding and profound fetal bradycardia immediately upon rupture of membranes.

items.q: Which rapid laboratory test can be performed at the bedside on vaginal blood to differentiate fetal blood from maternal blood in suspected vasa previa?
items.exp: The Apt (alkali denaturation) test is a rapid bedside test that differentiates fetal hemoglobin from maternal hemoglobin. Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is alkali-resistant: adding 1% sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to the lysed blood sample keeps it pink, confirming fetal origin. Adult maternal hemoglobin (HbA) denatures, turning brownish-yellow.
r: Correct. The Apt test differentiates alkali-resistant fetal hemoglobin (pink) from maternal hemoglobin (brown).
Incorrect. Kleihauer-Betke test quantifies fetomaternal hemorrhage in maternal blood, but takes hours to perform.
Incorrect. Direct Coombs test detects antibodies on red blood cells.
Incorrect. ESR is non-specific.
items.kp: The Apt test uses alkali denaturation to rapidly differentiate fetal blood (remains pink) from maternal blood (turns brown).

items.q: In a patient presenting with severe abruptio placentae, which blood product is most specifically indicated to replenish critical fibrinogen levels when serum fibrinogen is less than 100 mg/dL?
items.exp: In obstetric coagulopathy and DIC associated with placental abruption, consumption of fibrinogen is the hallmark hemostatic failure. Cryoprecipitate is highly concentrated in fibrinogen (providing 200-250 mg per unit) and factor VIII/vWF, making it the blood product of choice to rapidly restore plasma fibrinogen levels above the target threshold of 200 mg/dL.
r: Correct. Cryoprecipitate contains concentrated fibrinogen, making it first-line to correct hypofibrinogenemia in DIC.
Incorrect. Packed red cells restore oxygen-carrying capacity, but contain minimal fibrinogen.
Incorrect. Platelets correct thrombocytopenia, but contain negligible fibrinogen.
Incorrect. Albumin provides oncotic pressure but contains no clotting factors.
items.kp: Cryoprecipitate is the treatment of choice to rapidly replenish fibrinogen (target > 200 mg/dL) in severe DIC.

items.q: At what gestational age is planned elective cesarean delivery recommended for asymptomatic women with confirmed, persistent placenta previa covering the internal os?
items.exp: RCOG and ACOG guidelines recommend planned cesarean delivery between 36+0 and 37+6 weeks gestation for women with uncomplicated, asymptomatic placenta previa. This timing balances the risk of spontaneous labor and catastrophic antepartum hemorrhage against the risks of neonatal respiratory morbidity.
r: Correct. Delivery between 36+0 and 37+6 weeks balances bleeding prevention against neonatal prematurity.
Incorrect. 34-35 weeks is too early for asymptomatic previa, causing avoidable prematurity.
Incorrect. 39-40 weeks carries high risk of spontaneous labor and massive hemorrhage before surgery.
Incorrect. Post-term delivery is completely contraindicated in placenta previa.
items.kp: Planned cesarean delivery for uncomplicated placenta previa is recommended between 36+0 and 37+6 weeks gestation.

items.q: What is the primary maternal indication for emergency operative delivery in a patient presenting with moderate placental abruption at 33 weeks gestation?
o: Hemodynamic instability refractory to resuscitation or ongoing severe maternal hemorrhage
items.exp: Immediate emergency delivery in placental abruption is mandated by maternal hemodynamic instability refractory to volume replacement, severe uncontrollable ongoing hemorrhage, or fetal distress on CTG, regardless of gestational age. If mother and fetus are stable, conservative expectant management with corticosteroids can be considered before 34 weeks.
r: Correct. Maternal hemodynamic instability or refractory hemorrhage mandates emergency delivery.
Incorrect. Prematurity is a reason for conservative management if mother and fetus are stable.
Incorrect. Absence of labor is not an indication for emergency operative delivery.
Incorrect. Longitudinal lie is normal.
items.kp: Maternal hemodynamic compromise or active refractory hemorrhage mandates emergency delivery in placental abruption.

items.q: What ultrasound distance between the internal cervical os and the leading placental edge at 32 weeks gestation allows a trial of vaginal delivery without planned cesarean section?
o: Placental edge greater than 20 mm from the internal os
Placental edge directly covering the internal os
Placental edge within 5 mm of the internal os
Placental edge within 10 mm of the internal os
items.exp: A leading placental edge > 20 mm from the internal cervical os on transvaginal ultrasound in the third trimester is classified as a normal placental location and permits a safe trial of vaginal delivery, with low bleeding risk. When the edge is between 10 and 20 mm, vaginal delivery can be attempted in selected cases, but < 10 mm or previa mandates cesarean section.
r: Correct. A distance > 20 mm from the internal os on transvaginal scan permits safe vaginal delivery.
Incorrect. Placenta covering the internal os requires planned cesarean delivery.
Incorrect. Distance < 10 mm carries high risk of hemorrhage, warranting cesarean delivery.
Incorrect. Distance < 20 mm requires individualized assessment and carries higher bleeding risk.
items.kp: A placental edge greater than 20 mm from the internal cervical os safely permits a trial of vaginal delivery.
